To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) skeletonization is a viable option to achieve sparsity in neural networks and (2) the performance of the pruned networks can be significantly improved by considering the trainability of the parameters.
(i) we can skeletonize the networks at initialization, and (ii) we can do so at high pruning levels (up to 99.9%) while maintaining their performance.

(1) pruning beyond a certain level (approx 95%) of sparsity leads to performance degradation; (2) we propose a new objective (FORCE) to find the skeletonized network with the maximum foresight connection sensitivities, and (3) we show that our objective can be approximately maximized by two iterative approaches, Iterative SNIP and FORCE, which provide remarkably improved performance over other recent approaches
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (1) How to prune a neural network to a very high sparsity (99.5% of parameters) without degrading its performance? (2) How to prune parameters with a high foresight connection sensitivity?
two aspects of skeletonization: (1) finding a skeletonized network which is trainable and (2) finding a skeleton which provides maximum performance.
the following: (1) How to find a skeleton network that maximally retains the trainability of the network (2) How to iteratively prune the network while retaining the trainability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in terms of performance, skeletonization is a much more effective way to remove fat than random pruning.
our approach is a better choice than other approaches for skeletonization, and is especially useful when one wants to remove more than 95% of the parameters from a network.
our approach is the first to show that a pruned network can be as trainable as a dense network, and that the network performance can be improved even after pruning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our approach is the first to provide a systematic framework to find a sparse network that is trainable, while preserving its performance.

our method is the first to provide a practical way to remove more fat from networks at initialization, and to our knowledge, is the only approach to provide a practical solution to the problem of pruning beyond the 90-95% level of parameter reduction.
, we provide the first objective to find the best skeletonized network at initialization, and propose two efficient algorithms to maximize this objective.
The main takeaway from our work is that
pruning at initialization should be viewed as a two-step process where one first removes a large chunk of parameters and then fine-tunes the network to remove more parameters.
the trainability of the network needs to be considered in the skeletonization process.
, while pruning is a good way to reduce the number of parameters in a network, the performance of a pruned model depends on the order in which the parameters are pruned.
